title: CFA Ethics 25: Standard V(B) - separating fact from opinion when you talk to a client
subtitle: State the process, the limits of the model, and what has changed since last time
whyItMatters: Most client complaints do not come from losing money. They come from losing money in a way the client did not understand and was never warned about. Standard V(B) is the standard that addresses exactly that gap.
openingQuestion: Your report says: 'The company will deliver 25% revenue growth next year as the new plant comes online.' Where is the problem?
openingOptions: No problem, if your analysis genuinely produces that number
The sentence presents a forecast as though it were fact
The problem is that 25% is too precise to be reliable
The problem is not citing a source for the new plant
explanation: The word 'will' makes all the difference. That the plant is coming online may be a disclosed fact; the 25% figure is always an opinion, however carefully the model behind it was built. Standard V(B) requires you to keep the two apart, because clients read them in completely different ways and make different decisions as a result. The Standard's second requirement goes further: you must state the process and the limits of the analysis - what the model assumes, which assumption it is most sensitive to, and what would change the conclusion. A client who knows the forecast hinges on input prices reacts very differently when input prices spike.

summary.keyIdea: Clients read a fact and an opinion in completely different ways, so blending the two into one sentence transfers judgement risk to them without their knowing it.
summary.commonMistake: Using the language of certainty for a forecast. 'The company will grow 20%' is an opinion written as a fact.

application.title: How to write it safely
application.message: Split the sentence: let the fact stand alone, and open the opinion with the basis it rests on. The reader must be able to tell where they are trusting the data and where they are trusting you.

sections.text: Standard V(B) requires you to separate fact from opinion when communicating with clients. It sounds obvious, but a single word is enough to blur the line.
One word - 'will' - is all it takes

That the plant comes online next quarter may be a disclosed fact. A 25% rise in profit is always an opinion, however carefully the model behind it was built. Writing 'profit will rise 25%' instead of 'we estimate profit rises around 25%' has turned a forecast into an assertion - and a client decides quite differently depending on which of the two they read.

sections.label: The second requirement goes further
sections.text: You must state the process and the limits of the analysis: what the model assumes, which assumption it is most sensitive to, and what would change the conclusion. A client who knows the forecast hinges on input prices reacts very differently when input prices spike.

A change in analytical method or in the model itself has to be reported to the client, even when performance is still good. The reason is that clients judge a result through their understanding of how it was produced; change the how without saying so and they are reading a number against an out-of-date frame of reference.

With clients who have little financial experience the duty does not shrink, it changes shape: simplify the language, not the content. Dropping the risk section because you fear the client will not follow it is a breach, not a kindness.

lines: A client is entitled to know how sure you actually are.
And that is something only you can tell them.

diagram.label: Separate fact clearly from your own opinion
State the process and the main assumptions behind it
State the limits: what would change the conclusion
Report it when the process or the assumptions change

realWorldExample.company: The duty to report a change in process
realWorldExample.description: Standard V(B) does not apply only at the first presentation. If the investment process changes - a different valuation model, different stock-selection criteria, a different maximum leverage - the client has to be told, even when performance is still good. The reason is that the client chose you on the basis of a specific process; changing it without saying so alters the product they bought without asking them.

quiz.question: Which two things does Standard V(B) require you to keep clearly apart?
options: Historical data and forward-looking forecast data
A fact and the analyst's own opinion about it
Individual clients and institutional clients
Fundamental analysis and technical analysis
quiz.explanation: A client reads a fact and an opinion in entirely different ways, so mixing them corrupts the decision they are trying to make. The other splits listed here are real distinctions, but none of them is what V(B) is about: past versus forecast data still leaves the forecast dressed as certainty, the client type changes how you phrase things and not what you owe, and the choice between fundamental and technical work is a methodology question the Standard is indifferent to.

quiz.question: Why must you state the limits of an analytical model?
options: Because regulation requires a risk warning in every report
To reduce the analyst's legal exposure when a forecast misses
So the client knows what would make the conclusion change
So the client can rebuild the same model for themselves
quiz.explanation: The purpose is to let the client react correctly when conditions shift, not to shield the analyst - though it does happen to do that too. Framing it as a compliance box tends to produce boilerplate nobody reads, framing it as legal protection puts your interest ahead of the client's, and handing over enough for a full rebuild is neither required nor, for most clients, of any use. What matters is that they know where the conclusion is fragile.

quiz.question: The investment process changes but performance is still good. What then?
options: Only tell them if the management fee changes as well
No need - the duty only arises when results deteriorate
Just note it in the fund's next annual report to investors
Still tell them; the client chose that specific process
quiz.explanation: Changing the process without saying so changes the product the client bought without asking them, and a good result does not make that legitimate - it merely delays the moment the client discovers it. The duty is not triggered by underperformance, it is not tied to the fee schedule, and deferring it to the next annual report leaves the client holding a position they no longer understand for however many months that takes.

quiz.question: What is happening when you write 'the company will grow 25%' instead of 'we estimate 25%'?
options: Presenting an opinion as though it were an established fact
An accepted way to write concisely in a research report
Purely a question of house style, engaging no Standard at all
A breach of Standard I(C) on misrepresenting qualifications
quiz.explanation: One word changes how the client reads the whole sentence, and that is precisely what Standard V(B) targets: not prose style but what the reader ends up believing. Brevity is a poor defence when the shorter version asserts more than the analysis supports. And this is not Standard I(C) territory - nothing here misstates the analyst's own credentials; what is misstated is the confidence level of the number.

quiz.question: How does the duty change for a retail client with little experience?
options: Lighter, since the client lacks the background for technical detail
Unchanged in substance; the wording must fit their understanding
Heavier - the full quantitative model must be laid out for them
It does not apply; this Standard covers institutional clients only
quiz.explanation: Communicating to someone who cannot follow you is not yet communicating. Simplifying the language is mandatory; dropping the content is not. Treating inexperience as a reason to say less inverts the Standard, since it is exactly the least experienced client who most needs the risk explained. Burying them in the full quantitative model fails in the other direction, and no version of V(B) is reserved for institutions.

keyTakeaways: Separate fact from opinion - clients read the two in completely different ways
State the process, the main assumptions, and what would change the conclusion
Report a change in process, even when performance is still good
One 'will' in place of 'we estimate' is enough to turn an opinion into a fact
For inexperienced clients: simplify the language, never cut the content

practicePrompt.question: You are using a valuation model whose output is highly sensitive to the long-term growth assumption. How should you present it to the client?
options: Give only the final figure so the client is not confused
State clearly which assumption the result depends on most
Hand over the whole spreadsheet so the client can check it
Pick the most conservative assumption and report only that
practicePrompt.explanation: The other three are three different forms of evasion: hiding the fragility, dumping the whole problem on the client, or deciding on their behalf how cautious they should be. The correct answer hands over exactly what the client needs - knowing where the result is fragile - without making them read the model. A sensitivity table is the standard way of doing it.
